p.seg: As for sages who attain the Dao,
they are Huáng-Lǎo.
As for sages who govern the world,
they are Zhōu and Kǒng.
The Yellow Emperor first governed the world and then ascended to immortality;
this is a rare case of someone possessing the talent to do both.
Of the ancient emperors and kings
who carved inscriptions on Mount Tài,
it is possible to read about seventy-two families;
as for the others that have been worn away,
they are too numerous to count.
The fact that only the Yellow Emperor's immortality is recorded
makes it clear that this was carefully considered.
People take what someone excels at particularly,
what others cannot match,
and then call them a sage.
Therefore, one who is incomparably good at Weiqi (Go)
is called a "Sage of Go,"
hence Yán Zǐqīng and Mǎ Suí míng now have the name "Sage of Go."
One who is exceptionally good at historical writing
is called a "Sage of Calligraphy,"
hence Huáng Xiàng and Hú Zhāo now have the name "Sage of Calligraphy."
One who is exceptionally good at painting
is called a "Sage of Painting,"
hence Wèi Xié and Zhāng Mò now have the name "Sage of Painting."
One who is especially skilled at carving
is called a "Sage of Woodworking,"
hence Zhāng Héng and Mǎ Jūn now have the name "Sage of Woodworking."
Therefore, Mèngzǐ said that Bó Yí
was a sage of purity;
Liǔxià Huì
was a sage of harmony;
Yī Yǐn
was a sage of responsibility.
If I try to elaborate and discuss it,
then sagehood is not one single thing.
Now, Bān Shū, Chuí Dí,
were sages of mechanics;
Fù Biǎn, Hé Huǎn,
were sages of healing;
Zǐ Wéi, Gān Jūn,
were sages of astrology;
Shǐ Sū, Xīn Liào,
were sages of divination;
Xià Yù, Dù Huí,
were sages of physical strength;
Jīng Kē, Niè Zhèng,
were sages of courage;
Fēi Lián, Kuā Fù,
were sages of speed;
Zǐ Yě, Yán Zhōu,
were sages of discerning music;
Sūn Wú, Hán Bái,
were sages of military strategy.
"Sage"
is the highest title for human affairs;
This is not limited to literature alone.
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
"A robber possesses the Way of the sage in five aspects.
To presumptuously guess and know where people hide things is
intelligence;
to enter first without suspicion is
courage;
to come out last without fear is
righteousness;
to know what is appropriate to do or not is
wisdom;
to divide wealth equally is
benevolence.
There has never been a case of someone who did not possess these qualities becoming a great robber of the world."
Someone said:
"The Way of the sage
cannot be divided into branches and scattered leaves.
One must encompass all of it together
to be a sage."
I replied:
"Kǒngzǐ's disciples,
reaching seventy-two,
each attained one aspect of the sage's essence.
This means that sagely affairs can be divided.
Furthermore, it is said:
Yán Yuān possessed the whole body of the sage, but in miniature.
This means that sagely affairs have varying degrees of depth.
Furthermore, the *Yì* says:
"There are four ways of the sage:
in speech, he values its wording;
in action, he values its transformation;
in creating tools, he values their symbolism;
in divination, he values its prognostication."
This is clear proof that the way of the sage can be divided.
Why is it that those who excel in morality and virtue to achieve divine immortality
cannot be called sages who have attained the Dao?
If there are no sages who have attained the Dao,
then would Zhōu and Kǒng not be considered sages who govern the world?
Since they are not the same,
why should we demand that they combine?
According to the immortal scriptures, all those who attain immortality
receive their fate by coincidentally encountering the *qì* of deities and immortals,
naturally endowed.
Therefore, within the womb,
they already possess the nature of believing in the Dao.
When they become conscious,
they naturally love such matters.
They will surely encounter a wise teacher and obtain the method.
Otherwise,
they will neither believe nor seek,
and even if they seek, they will not obtain it.
The *Yùqián Jīng Zhǔmìng Yuán* says:
"A person's fortune, good or bad,
is determined on the day of conception and reception of *qì*,
when they receive the essence of the celestial constellations above.
If one corresponds to the star of a sage, then one will be a sage;
if one corresponds to the star of a worthy person, then one will be worthy;
if one corresponds to the star of a refined person, then one will be refined;
if one corresponds to the star of a martial person, then one will be martial;
if one corresponds to the star of a noble person, then one will be noble;
if one corresponds to the star of a wealthy person, then one will be wealthy;
if one corresponds to the star of a lowly person, then one will be lowly;
if one corresponds to the star of a poor person, then one will be poor;
if one corresponds to the star of longevity, then one will have longevity;
if one corresponds to the star of an immortal, then one will be an immortal.
Furthermore, there are stars of gods, immortals, and sages;
there are stars of sages who govern the world;
there are stars of those who combine two sage-like qualities;
there are stars of those who are noble but not wealthy;
there are stars of those who are wealthy but not noble;
there are stars of those who combine wealth and nobility;
there are stars of those who are wealthy first and then poor;
there are stars of those who are noble first and then lowly;
there are stars of those who combine poverty and lowliness;
there are stars of those whose wealth and nobility do not last;
there are stars of loyalty and filial piety;
there are stars of those who are fierce and evil.
Such things cannot be fully recorded;
this is a rough outline.
A person's life inherently has a fixed destiny,
as Zhāng Chēzi's 張車子 theory states.
If one does not receive the destiny of an immortal,
then one will certainly not have a fondness for immortality;
There has never been someone who dislikes something in their heart and yet seeks to do it;
there has never been someone who obtains something without seeking it.
From ancient times to the present,
there have been those of great talent and clear understanding
who do not believe in the existence of immortals,
and there have been those of mediocre ability who, by earnestly seeking, have attained immortality.
Jiǎ, though knowledgeable in many things, may be blinded to the truth of immortality;
Yǐ, though understanding little else, might profoundly comprehend its principles.
Is this not due to the decrees of destiny?
The Daoist school treasures its secret immortal arts;
among disciples,
it particularly emphasizes careful selection.
The essence is refined over a long period
and then revealed in crucial formulas.
All the more so with worldly people
who are fortunate enough to neither believe nor seek;
why should one forcibly try to tell them?
Not only can one not transform them to believe,
but one will also invite ridicule and hasten slander.
Therefore, those who have attained the Dao
walk a different path and
dwell in different places from ordinary people.
In speech, they do not wish to associate with them;
in person, they do not wish to mingle with them.
Separated by a thousand *lǐ*,
they still fear it is not enough to escape the onslaught of troubles;
cutting off all traces,
they still fear it is not enough to avoid the shame of being disgraced.
Rank is not enough to entice them,
wealth is not enough to move them,
why would they be willing to flaunt themselves before vulgar scholars,
and say that they have immortal methods?
This is probably why Zhōu Kǒng had no chance to know the Dao of Immortality.
Moreover, Zhōu Kǒng,
were profound and far-reaching scholars of high talent and great learning.
Even minor skills,
they often were not skilled in.
If they were made to juggle balls and play with swords,
jump over sword points and throw into narrow spaces,
tread and ascend flagpoles,
pick up plates and climb tables,
hang with their heels on sheer cliffs ten thousand *rèn* high,
swim in the unfathomable Lǚ Liáng rapids,
lift a thousand *jūn* with their hands,
step on startling whirlwinds with their feet,
violently seize tigers and capture leopards,
snatch flying swift arrows,
ordinary people can do these things,
but Zhōu Kǒng cannot,
how much more those things that surpass these?
Other people's contemplations,
what fleas are heading towards,
the high officials beyond the wall,
the weeds and trash under the forest,
the books in boxes and chests,
the treasures in the ground,
The birds and beasts in dense forests and deep thickets,
the fish and turtles in deep pools and vast ponds,
even if we were to ask Zhōu Kǒng to meticulously depict their colors,
and distinguish their species,
to list their quantities in the classics,
and verify their existence,
they might not be able to know them all completely.
How much more so those who are far removed from them?
Sages, if they do not eat, become hungry;
if they do not drink, become thirsty;
if burned, feel heat;
if frozen, feel cold;
if struck, feel pain;
if cut, are wounded;
with age, they grow old;
if injured, they become sick;
when their breath is cut off, they die.
In these ways, they share much with ordinary people,
and the ways in which they differ are few.
That which sets them far above others
lies solely in their talent, far-reaching thought,
eloquent speech, and soaring penmanship,
complete virtue, and pure conduct,
the work of diligent instruction and extensive learning.
How could they possibly be versed in everything?
Having already composed canonical texts,
brought peace to the high and governed the people,
would you also have them understand the Dao of Immortals
To demand immortality
from sages,
how excessive is that?
I have heard that profound words offend common ears,
and truthful words must go against the crowd.
If Confucian scholars were to hastily read this book of mine,
they would surely say that I am defaming the sages.
How could I be so?
I only wish to fully explore the principles of things.
When the principles are exhausted and matters are thoroughly investigated,
it will then seem like I am slandering Zhōu Kǒng.
People of the world say that sages fell from the sky,
as if they were divine beings,
all-knowing,
and all-powerful.
They are even more in awe of their names,
and dare not re-examine them with facts.
If it's said that something was not done by a sage,
then no one would be able to do it;
if it's said that a sage didn't know something,
then no one would be able to know it either.
Isn't that laughable?
Now I will use recent events to compare,
hoping it can bring enlightenment.
The birds of Wánshān,
their cries sound like selling life and sending off the dead,
Kǒngzǐ did not know about them.
Could it then be said that Yán Huí could only partially understand them?
I heard the crying of a woman from Mount Tài [Tài Shān].
I asked about it.
Then I learned that a tiger had eaten three members of her family.
I still didn't understand why this woman didn't move away.
Only after needing an answer did I realize.
I saw someone netting sparrows and only catching nestlings [huáng kǒu].
I couldn't discern the meaning behind it.
Only after asking did I understand.
When I wanted to bury my mother,
I didn't know where my father's grave was located.
I needed someone to tell me.
After fixing the tomb, it collapsed.
Again, I didn't understand it.
My disciple advised me.
Then I burst into tears.
Furthermore, I suspected Yán Yuān [Yán Yuān] of stealing food.
Thus, I falsely said I wanted to offer a sacrifice to my ancestors.
I used divination and dusting to reveal his falsehood.
The stable burned down.
Again, I didn't know if anyone or any horses were injured.
After Yán Yuān [Yán Yuān] arrived,
I declared that he had died.
Furthermore, I traveled to over seventy states,
yet I couldn't foresee that people would definitely not employ me.
So I was restless and hurried,
never allowing my mat to get warm.
I also didn't know that the people of Kuāng [Kuāng] would surround me,
yet I took that route.
He asked Lǎozǐ about ancient rites,
but there were aspects of the rites he didn't understand.
He asked Tánzǐ about bird-named officials,
but there were officials he didn't recognize.
Traveling without knowing the ferry crossing,
and asking someone about it,
and yet not knowing the person being asked,
they will surely mock him and not tell him the way,
in which case it is obvious that one should not ask.
To get out of the carriage and chase after a singing phoenix,
and not realize that it won't stay.
To see Nánzǐ and not realize that it's of no benefit.
Such things like these
cannot be fully enumerated,
but not knowing the methods of immortality,
what is there to be surprised about?
Furthermore, vulgar scholars say:
"What the sages cannot do,
then everyone else cannot do."
But the Dàng people live on the water,
the Liáng mother was transformed by fire,
Bózǐ could endure extreme heat,
Zhòngdū could withstand extreme cold,
Zuǒ Cí used the method of "corpse liberation" and did not die,
Gān Shǐ abstained from grains and lived through the year,
Fàn Yì was struck but not penetrated,
Biē Líng had his corpse float downstream and was reborn,
Shǎoqiān controlled hundreds of ghosts,
Cháng Fáng shrank the earth's veins;
Zhòng Fǔ transformed his form into a morning wild duck;
Zhāng Kǎi blew and puffed, creating clouds and mist.
I have not heard of Zhōu or Kǒng being able to do such things."
Common people sometimes say,
"Zhōu and Kǒng could all do this,
but they just didn't do it."
I answered them,
"If we do not seek it in clear writings,
but point to it with empty words,
then I can also say that Zhōu and Kǒng could flap their wings and soar,
fly around the eight extremes,
raise clouds and bring rain,
move mountains and uproot wells,
but they just didn't do it.
If we do not base things on what is seen in recorded books,
then what limit is there?
If it is as you say,
I can also say that Zhōu and Kǒng have already ascended to become immortals,
but this method cannot be used to instruct the world,
for fear that people would all know that immortality is attainable,
and all would certainly entrust all their offerings,
abandon advancing in office and climb dangerous floats into deep places,
in order to cultivate this path,
resulting in families having no descendants,
and the state having no officials,
loyalty and filial piety both being lost,
and the great relationships would certainly be disordered.
Therefore, Zhōu and Kǒng secretly cultivated it themselves,
and kept it a secret from others.
Outwardly, they feigned the appearance of final demise,
while inwardly possessing the reality of transcendent immortality.
If this is so,
then what can you use to challenge me?
It may very well be true.
The Língbǎo Scripture contains three chapters: "Correct Opportunity Balance," "Flying Turtle," and "Transmission of Secrets,"
all of which are immortal arts.
The King of Wú quarried stone to build palaces,
and within the joined stones,
he obtained books written in purple script on golden tablets.
Unable to read them,
he sent a messenger to ask Zhòngní,
deceiving Zhòngní by saying:
"The King of Wú was at leisure,
when a red sparrow carried a book in its beak and placed it on the palace hall.
Not knowing its meaning,
we have come from afar to consult you."
Zhòngní looked at it
and said:
"This is the method of Língbǎo,
the way to long life,
practiced by Yǔ,
hidden in the land of water,
whose years equal Heaven and Earth,
and who pays homage in the Purple Court.
When Yǔ was about to become an immortal,
It was sealed within a stone box on a famous mountain,
and now a red sparrow carries it,
it is likely a gift from heaven.
Judging by this, Xià Yǔ did not die,
and Zhòng Ní knew about it;
how do we know that Zhòng Ní did not secretly cultivate the same Dao?
Even if we assume the sages did not do this,
we cannot say there was no effect.
People's likes and dislikes
are all different.
If you explain it to them face to face,
how could they not believe it?
If it truly aligns with their intentions,
even if it is small, they will do it;
if it does not accord with their spirit,
even if it is great, they will not learn it.
Some like bitterness and dislike sweetness,
and these kinds of preferences already exist;
there are also countless cases of people who are greedy for profit and abandon righteousness.
yì wú shù yān.
"The great treasure of a sage is called position,
what is used to gather people is called wealth."
It is also said:
"Wealth and honor
are what people desire,"
but in the past, there were already those who were offered the throne of an emperor but did not accept it,
were entrusted with the wealth of the four seas but did not desire it,
scorned the officials of the three dignitaries and the nine ministers,
turned their backs on gifts of jade and silk,
pursued the high purity of mountains and forests,
and were content with the humble profession of fishing and angling.
Indeed, these are too numerous to count.
It is also said:
"Men and women, eating and drinking,
are the greatest desires of humankind.'
Therefore, fondness for beauty cannot be dissuaded,
and delicious flavors can cause one to forget worries.
In the past, there were those who abstained from grains and rejected beauty,
did not keep wives and concubines,
transcended the world and went alone,
were filled with joy,
gazed at their reflections and felt happiness,
rinsed their mouths with streams and forgot the taste of food,
and these are too numerous to record.
Human nature invariably loves fair faces and beautiful figures,
light bodies and gentle forms,
yet the Yellow Emperor sought out the ugly Mómǔ,
and Marquis Chén pitied the detestable Dūnqià.
Everyone's nose enjoys fragrance,
therefore ambergris and turmeric, orchids and storax, bear's gall and plain gum, *Jiangli* and *Jieche*, spring orchids and autumn orchids,
were valued as highly as jade,
yet the women on the coast
pursued husbands with terrible odors,
and followed them without ceasing.
Zhōu Wén was fond of unappetizing pickles,
and would not trade them for the flavors of a grand sacrificial offering.
Wèi Míng (魏明) favored the sound of chisels and gouges,
and would not exchange it for the harmony of string and bamboo instruments.
People each have their own preferences,
how can one demand that this be the same as that?
Zhōu (周) and Kǒng (孔) lived solitary lives,
and did not believe in the Dao of Immortals.
There are places where the sun and moon do not shine,
and things that even sages do not know.
How can one say that there are no Immortals in the world
simply because sages do not pursue it!
That would be like blaming the sun, moon, and stars for not shining inside an inverted bowl."
Someone asked,
"The Immortals of ancient times,
did they all attain their abilities through learning,
or were they simply born with extraordinary qi?"
Bàopǔzǐ (抱朴子) replied,
"What are you saying?
Did they not all carry their books and follow teachers,
accumulating diligence and effort,
enduring frost and braving danger,
combing the wind and bathing in the rain,
and personally undertaking sweeping and cleaning?
They experienced hardship and exhausting labor,
initially showing themselves through trustworthiness and action,
and ultimately being tested with danger and difficulty.
If their nature was sincere and their conduct steadfast,
their hearts without resentment or disloyalty,
then they were permitted to ascend the hall and enter the inner chamber.
Some become lazy and weary and stop halfway;
some harbor resentment and anger and then retreat;
some are seduced by glory and profit;
and return to practicing the affairs of common custom;
some are defeated by heterodox theories;
and lose their ambition for plainness and simplicity;
some act in the morning and desire its completion by evening;
some sit in cultivation and immediately expect results.
As for those who see wealth and beauty and whose hearts do not tremble,
and hear worldly talk and whose wills are not disheartened,
among ten thousand men,
even having one such person is considered many.
Therefore, those who attempt it are as numerous as the hairs of an ox,
but those who attain it are as rare as the horn of a *qílín*.
Now, drawing a strong crossbow,
relies on the power to release the arrow;
crossing a great river,
depends on preserving oneself through having already crossed;
a well that does not reach the spring
is as if it were not dug at all;
a single step not yet reached
is as if one has not yet set out.
The accumulation of a long journey
is not achieved in a short time;
the height of soaring to the heavens
is not built by a single basket of earth.
However, those climbing steep slopes worry about falling short at the top due to insufficient strength,
those pursuing the *Dào* suffer from an ambition unfulfilled just as it is about to be accomplished.
Thousands of granaries and myriad storehouses
are not the product of a single plowing.
A tree reaching to the heavens
does not grow in ten days.
An unfathomable abyss
originates from trickling rivulets.
The wealth of Táo Zhū
must be accumulated by the hundreds and thousands.
If one retreats when others advance,
this is how Yīn Zǐ ultimately fathomed the Dao.
Maintaining reverence from beginning to end,
this is how Xiàn Mén attained the cloud-dragon.
My will is truly firm,
what kind of person is he?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The common people are unable to generate life,
yet devote themselves to what kills life.
Things that are finite
cannot supply limitless consumption.
The flow of rivers
cannot fill a bottomless vessel.
Even those whose income is small and expenses are high
still find themselves unable to make ends meet.
How much more so when there is no income, even a tiny amount,
but thousands and hundreds spent?
People, regardless of age,
all have illnesses,
it's just a matter of degree.
And the amount of *qì* one receives varies.
Those with more exhaust it slowly,
those with less exhaust it quickly.
Those who understand the Way replenish and rescue it,
first restoring it to its original state,
and only then seeking additional benefits to its measurable manifestations.
If you were to take medicines all day long,
your flesh would fly and your bones would soar;
if you were to guide and stretch and change the calendar,
your feathers and wings would be uneven.
Then there would be no one in the world who did not believe in the Way.
The problem is that the benefit of small gains is not yet firm,
while the expenses of large losses follow one after another.
The foundation is not yet fully established,
while the poison of ice and frost attack simultaneously.
Not knowing that the fault lies within oneself,
one instead claims that the Way is of no benefit,
and thus abandons pills and powders and ceases expelling and intaking.
Therefore, it is said: It is not that long life is difficult,
but that hearing the Way is difficult.
It is not that hearing the Way is difficult,
but that practicing it is difficult.
It is not that practicing it is difficult,
but that persisting in it is difficult.
A good craftsman can give people rulers and compasses,
but cannot make people certainly skillful.
A wise teacher can impart prescriptions,
but cannot make people certainly follow them.
Cultivating the Dao is like planting grain;
achieving it is like gathering and storing the harvest.
Though the fields may be fertile,
and the water sources abundant,
if one's efforts miss the opportune time,
and the plowing and weeding are insufficient,
even if the emerging crops cover the ridges,
without harvesting and reaping,
though the area of land is vast,
one will still have no yield.
Generally, people not only fail to recognize what benefits are beneficial,
but also fail to recognize what detriments are detrimental.
Detriment is easily known and comes quickly,
while benefit is difficult to know and comes slowly.
People still do not awaken to what is easy;
how can they recognize what is difficult?
That which diminishes resembles a lamp's fire consuming its oil,
no one sees it,
yet suddenly it is exhausted.
That which benefits resembles the planting and growing of seedlings,
no one perceives it,
yet suddenly they flourish.
Therefore, in governing oneself and nourishing one's nature,
one must be careful in the details.
One must not fail to cultivate the Dao because of small benefits that seem insignificant,
nor fail to guard against small detriments that seem harmless.
Generally, accumulating small things leads to great achievements,
accumulating single units leads to reaching billions.
If one can cherish something in its nascent stages,
and accomplish it in the manifest,
then one is close to understanding it."
Someone asked:
"In ancient times, were there those who, without practicing any specific methods,
accidentally achieved longevity?"
Bàopǔzǐ answered:
"No.
Some followed enlightened masters,
accumulating merits and diligently toiling,
and then were granted compounded medicines.
Others received secret formulas,
personally engaged in preparation and refinement,
their affairs not connected with the world,
their words not encumbered by common customs.
Those who recorded such matters only preserved their names,
and were unable to fully know how they attained immortality;
thus, such details are omitted.
In the past, the Huángdì was born with the ability to speak
and commanded hundreds of spirits.
He can be considered to have possessed a body naturally endowed by heaven,
yet he still could not attain the Dao by simply sitting.
Therefore, he ascended Mount Wángwū to receive the Dān Jīng (Scripture of Elixir),
arrived at Dǐnghú (Cauldron Lake) to fly with Liúzhū (Flying Pearl),
climbed Mount Kōngtóng to inquire of Guǎngchéng (Master of Vast Accomplishment),
went to Mount Jùcí to serve Dàwěi,
traveled to East Dài to honor Zhōnghuáng (Central Yellow),
entered Jīngǔ (Golden Valley) to consult Juānzǐ (Master Juān),
To cultivate the Dao, he sought the help of the two women Xuán Sù 玄素;
for precise calculations and astronomical observations, he consulted Shān Jī 山稽 and Lì Mù 力牧;
when discussing divination and prognostication, he inquired of Fēng Hòu 風後;
when composing works on physical examination, he received instruction from Léi Qí 雷岐;
in carefully considering military attacks and defenses, he adopted the strategies of the Five Sounds;
to thoroughly understand divine treachery, he recorded the words of Bái Zé 白澤;
in assessing geomancy, he wrote down the theories of Qīng Wū 青烏;
and to heal injuries and disabilities, he compiled the techniques of metalworking.
Therefore, he was able to comprehensively cover secret essentials,
fully explore the Dao, and exhaustively understand truth.
Consequently, he ascended on a dragon to soar high,
becoming boundless like Heaven and Earth.
However, according to the scriptures of the immortals,
it is said that the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi both served the Tàiyǐ Yuánjūn 太乙元君 to receive essential formulas.
How much more so those who do not attain to those two lords,
how can they independently attain immortality and transcend the world?
Such a thing has not been heard of."
Someone asked:
"The Yellow Emperor, if he truly became an immortal,
what is the burial mound at Qiáoshān 橋山
for, then?"
Bàopǔzǐ 抱朴子 replied:
"According to the Jīng Shān Jīng 荊山經 and the Lóngshǒu Jì 龍首記,
both say that after the Yellow Emperor ingested divine elixirs,
a dragon came to greet him.
The assembled ministers, filled with longing and admiration,
were at a loss for what to do.
Some took his stools and staff,
They established temples to sacrifice to them;
or they took their clothes and hats,
buried them and guarded them.
The *Liè Xiān Zhuàn* says:
Huángdì chose his own day of death,
seventy days to depart,
seventy days to return,
and was buried at Qiáoshān.
The mountain tomb suddenly collapsed,
the tomb was empty with no corpse,
but only a sword and shoes were there.
Although these accounts differ,
they all agree on his becoming an immortal.
That Huángdì became an immortal
is found very often in Daoist texts and the sayings of various schools,
but the Ru scholars were unwilling to promote strange tales,
to open up different paths,
and focused on ritual teachings.
The affairs of gods and immortals
could not be used to instruct the common people,
so they said he died,
in order to stop the people's minds from wandering.
Zhū Yì, Luán Bā, and Yú Gōng,
had meritorious benefits for the people,
and the people all built temples to worship them while they were alive.
Moreover, in ancient times, people of great virtue,
after their death,
their ministers and sons carved their merits and achievements on imperishable vessels.
Nowadays, when rulers rise and fall,
and officials and commoners remember them with longing,
there are often those who erect steles praising their virtue.
This is similar to the case of the Yellow Emperor having temples and tombs.
Can this alone prove that they necessarily died?"
Someone asked:
"Péng Zǔ lived to eight hundred,
and Ān Qī to three thousand.
This is surpassing the lifespan of ordinary people.
If there truly is a way to immortality,
why didn't they achieve immortality?
Isn't it that they were endowed with destiny and vital energy,
and naturally had a lifespan of their own length?
They just happened to obtain more of it,
but in principle, it could not be extended,
so they could not avoid decay and death?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"According to the records of Péng Zǔ,
he served Yáo as an assistant to Emperor Kù,
and continued as a high official from the Xià to the Yīn dynasty.
The Yīn king sent maidens to learn the techniques of the bedchamber from him.
When they proved effective,
the king wanted to kill Péng Zǔ
to cut off his path.
Péng Zǔ became aware of this and fled.
He left when he was over seven or eight hundred years old,
so he did not die.
The *Huáng Shígōng Jì* (黃石公記) says:
More than seventy years after Péng Zǔ (彭祖) departed,
his disciples saw him west of the quicksand,
making it clear he did not die.
Furthermore, Péng Zǔ's (彭祖) disciples,

Qīngyī Wūgōng (青衣烏公), Hēi Xué Gōng (黑穴公), Xiùméi Gōng (秀眉公), the White Rabbit Gentleman (Bái Tù Gōngzǐ), Lílóu Gōng (離婁公), Tàizú Jūn (太足君), Gāoqiū Zǐ (高丘子), Bù Kěn Lái (不肯來) and seven or eight others,
all lived for several hundred years.
They all became immortals during the Yīn (殷) dynasty.
How could Péng Zǔ (彭祖) have possibly died?
Furthermore, Liú Xiàng's (劉向) recorded *Lièxiān Zhuàn* (列仙傳) also says that Péng Zǔ (彭祖) was an immortal.
Moreover, Master Ānqí (安期先生),
sold medicine by the seashore.
People of Lángyá (琅琊) passed down stories of seeing him for generations,
estimating that he had lived for a thousand years.
Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) asked to speak with him,
for three days and three nights.
His words were profound,
his intentions far-reaching,
broad and well-supported.
Shǐhuáng (始皇) was amazed by him,
and bestowed upon him gold and jade,
worth tens of millions.
Ānqí (安期) accepted it and placed it at the Fùxiāng (阜鄉) pavilion,
giving a pair of red jade shoes as repayment.
He left a letter saying,
"After several thousand years,
seek me on Mount Pénglái (蓬萊山)."
Therefore,
This means that when he was seen by Emperor Shǐ Huáng, he was already a thousand years old;
he did not die.
Moreover, Emperor Shǐ Huáng was rigid, violent, arrogant, and obstinate,
and was the least likely person in the world to believe in immortals.
Nor was he one who would accept a negative answer.
As for questioning Ān Qī about matters of longevity,
Ān Qī's answers were appropriate and fitting.
Emperor Shǐ Huáng became enlightened,
and believed that there must be immortal paths in the world.
He generously bestowed gifts,
and was willing to learn the art of immortality.
But he simply lacked a qualified teacher
and was deceived and played with by people like Lú Áo and Xú Fú,
so he could not obtain it.
If Master Ān Qī had spoken without evidence,
within three days and three nights,
he would have been completely cornered.
Then Emperor Shǐ Huáng would have certainly boiled and slaughtered him,
and he would not have escaped the calamity of the cooking pot and chopping board.
How could he have obtained the generous gifts?"
Someone asked:
"People take medicines,
practice circulating qi and guiding the body,
but still cannot avoid death.
Why is that?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"If one does not obtain the golden elixir,
but only takes herbal medicines and practices minor arts,
Can prolong life and delay death,
but will not attain immortality.
Perhaps one only knows to take herbal medicines,
but does not know the essential techniques for reversing aging,
then there will ultimately be no principle for long life.
Perhaps one does not understand wearing magical charms,
practicing prohibitions,
contemplating the spirits within the body,
guarding the true One,
then it can only prevent internal diseases from arising,
and prevent wind-dampness from invading.
If suddenly there are evil ghosts and powerful malevolent forces,
mountain spirits and water poisons harm them,
then they will simply die.
Perhaps one does not obtain the methods for entering the mountains,
causing the mountain gods to create calamity for them,
then demonic ghosts will test them,
fierce beasts will wound them,
stream poisons will strike them,
snakes and vipers will sting them,
leading to many deaths,
not just one type.
Perhaps one cultivates the Dao late in life,
and has already deeply injured oneself beforehand,
making it difficult to restore and repair.
The benefits of restoration and repair
have not yet taken root,
and illnesses recur,
Therefore, how could acts of conquest and aggression
possibly lead to longevity?
Some become immortals when old through cultivating the Dao,
while others fail to achieve it when young, despite practicing the Dao.
Why is this?
Those who are old, though old, received a substantial endowment of *qì* at birth.
If the initial endowment of *qì* is plentiful, then the damage sustained is slight.
If the damage is slight, then it is easy to nourish.
Because it is easy to nourish, they attain immortality.
These, though young, received a small initial endowment of *qì*.
If the initial endowment of *qì* is small, then the harm is deep.
If the harm is deep, then it is difficult to remedy.
Because it is difficult to remedy, they do not achieve immortality.
The *mùjǐn* (hibiscus) and willow,
when cuttings are planted, they revive.
If felled, they still live.
If laid sideways, they still live.
Nothing is easier to bring to life
than these trees.
However, if buried shallowly,
and not for long,
constantly carved and stripped,
or shaken or uprooted,
even if enriched with fertile soil
and soaked with spring rain,
they still cannot escape withering,
because their roots are not firm,
and they have no time to sprout,
The body fluids cannot adequately congeal and sustain its vitality.
The human body,
is easily damaged and difficult to nourish.
Comparing it to two trees,
it cannot last long.
And what destroys it,
is excessive carving and stripping,
as severe as shaking and uprooting.
Those who help it are few,
those who ruin it are many,
thus death is fitting.
Now, expelling the old and taking in the new,
relies on qi to nourish qi,
but when qi is greatly weakened, it is difficult to nourish.
Taking medicinal foods,
relies on blood to replenish blood,
but when blood is about to be exhausted, it is difficult to replenish.
Now, panting and gasping after running,
or coughing or feeling full,
exerting effort and laboring the body,
eagerly short of strength,
are signs of qi depletion.
A face without radiance,
skin that is withered and dry,
parched lips and pale pulse,
and shriveled pores,
are symptoms of blood depletion.
When these two signs are weakened externally,
then the spiritual root also withers within.
In this condition,
without obtaining superior medicine,
it cannot be saved.
All those who practice the Dao but fail,
and strive for life but obtain death,
it is not that they do not have *qì* and blood.
However, that which constitutes *qì* and blood within the body,
its root source is already lost,
only branches and streams remain.
It is like a piece of burnt-out wood in the water,
the fire is extinguished, but the smoke does not immediately cease;
or a tree that has already been cut down,
the branches and leaves still grow.
It is not that these two do not have smoke,
it is not that they do not have leaves,
but that which makes them smoke and leaves,
has already perished beforehand.
People of the world, from the day they become aware of illness,
only then begin to treat it as a disease,
it is just like the day the breath is cut off,
only then is considered the time when the body perishes.
They only blame wind-cold, and heat-dampness,
not knowing that wind-cold and heat-dampness,
cannot harm a robust and strong person,
it is only those who suffer from body weakness and *qì* deficiency,
who cannot endure it,
and are therefore struck by it.
How can we compare them?
Let us suppose there are several people,
whose ages, old and young, are the same,
and whose food and clothing are of equal thickness and thinness.
They all go to a desert place,
and all brave the severe cold of night.
Pure snow falls from above,
and black ice freezes below.
The cold wind breaks branches and terrifies the night,
and coughs and spit freeze on the lips.
Then among them, there will be some who are particularly susceptible to the cold,
but not necessarily all will become ill.
It is not that the cold air is biased,
but that some people's bodies are less tolerant.
Therefore, if all eat the same thing,
but only some become ill from it,
it is not that this thing is particularly poisonous.
If all drink from the same vessels,
and some become sober while others become drunk,
it is not that the power of the wine is different for each person.
If all brave the scorching heat,
and some alone die from sunstroke,
it is not that the heat of the heavens has partiality.
If all take the same medicine,
and some become dizzy and irritable,
it is not that the poison has likes and dislikes.
Therefore, when a strong wind rushes through the forest,
the withered branches break first;
Great waves surge against the cliffs,
causing those with cracks and weak points to collapse first.
A raging fire sweeps across the plains,
and dry grass is burned before anything else.
A dragon bowl falls to the ground,
and only the fragile one shatters.
Judging from this,
when a person is without the Dao,
their body is already inherently weak.
They are merely being triggered by wind, cold, heat, or dampness.
If one can ensure that the vital energy (zhèng qì) does not decline,
and that the body and spirit protect each other,
nothing can harm them.
Generally, those who pursue the Dao
are always troubled by starting late,
not troubled by starting early.
Relying on youthful vigor
and robust physical strength,
they overexert themselves,
accumulating a multitude of ailments.
Their lives become as precarious as morning dew.
Lacking access to great medicine,
and only taking herbs and plants,
they may recover better than ordinary people,
but they cannot extend their natural lifespan.
Therefore, the Immortal Scripture says:
"Nurturing life is fundamentally about avoiding injury."
This is an essential saying.
Shén Nóng said:
"If hundreds of illnesses are not cured,
how can one attain longevity?
Truly, these words are believable."
Someone asked:
"The things that harm us,
are they not related to excessive indulgence in desires?"
Bàopǔzi said:
"How could it be only this?
However, the key to longevity
lies in the methods of reversing the aging process.
Superior people know this,
and can extend their years and eliminate illness.
The next best are those who do not deplete themselves.
If one is still young and vigorous and knows how to reverse aging,
takes Yīn Dān to nourish the brain,
and gathers the Yù Yè from the long valleys,
without taking medicines,
they still will not fail to live three hundred years,
but they will only not become immortals.
For those who do not grasp the technique,
the ancients compared them to holding hot soup in an ice cup,
or storing fire in a feather pouch.
Moreover, if one's talent cannot reach a certain level,
yet one racks one's brains,
it is harmful;
if one's strength cannot bear a certain weight,
yet one forcibly lifts it,
Injurious.
Grief and emaciation are
injurious.
Excessive joy and pleasure are
injurious.
Greedily pursuing desires is
injurious.
Prolonged talking and laughter are
injurious.
Sleeping and resting at irregular times are
injurious.
Drawing bows and pulling crossbows are
injurious.
Excessive drinking to the point of vomiting is
injurious.
Lying down immediately after a full meal is
injurious.
Jumping, running, and panting with exhaustion are
injurious.
Loud cheering and weeping are
injurious.
Failure of *yīn* and *yáng* to interact is
injurious.
Accumulating injuries to the point of exhaustion leads to premature death;
premature death is not the proper way.
Therefore, in the methods of nourishing life:
do not spit far;
do not walk with quick steps;
Do not strain your ears to the extreme when listening.
Do not strain your eyes by looking for too long.
Do not sit for an excessive amount of time.
Do not lie down to the point of exhaustion.
Put on clothes before feeling extremely cold.
Take off clothes before feeling extremely hot.
Do not eat when extremely hungry.
Eat no more than full.
Do not drink when extremely thirsty.
Drink no more than necessary.
In general, excessive eating leads to accumulation and stagnation.
Excessive drinking leads to the formation of phlegm and obstructions.
Do not engage in excessive labor or excessive leisure.
Do not wake up late.
Do not sweat profusely.
Do not sleep too much.
Do not race in carriages or run on horseback.
Do not strain your eyes by gazing far into the distance.
Do not consume an excessive amount of raw and cold foods.
Do not drink wine in the wind.
Do not bathe too frequently.
Do not hold vast ambitions or distant aspirations.
Do not scheme to create strange and ingenious things.
In winter, do not seek extreme warmth.
In summer, do not seek excessive coolness.
Do not sleep exposed under the stars.
Do not sleep with your shoulders uncovered.
Extreme cold and extreme heat,
Great wind and great fog,
one should not wish to brave them.
When the five flavors enter the mouth,
one should not wish for one to be excessively prevalent,
therefore, excessive sourness injures the Spleen,
excessive bitterness injures the Lungs,
excessive spiciness injures the Liver,
excessive saltiness injures the Heart,
excessive sweetness injures the Kidneys.
This is the natural principle of the Five Elements (wǔ xíng).
Whenever we speak of "injury,"
it is not something immediately felt;
it means that over time, it diminishes one's lifespan.
Therefore, those who are good at nourishing life
have early and late times for sleeping and waking, according to the four seasons;
their actions and dwelling have constant regulations of perfect harmony;
for regulating and benefiting the muscles and bones,
there are methods of bending and stretching;
for preventing disease and blocking out evil influences,
there are techniques of inhaling and exhaling;
for circulating *róng* and *wèi* (nutritive and defensive energies),
there are methods of tonifying and draining;
for regulating labor and rest,
there is the essential principle of giving and taking.
Endure anger to preserve the *yīn qì* (陰氣, feminine/passive energy),
suppress joy to nourish the *yáng qì* (陽氣, masculine/active energy).
Then, first take herbs and plants to remedy deficiencies,
and later take golden elixir (jīn dān) to secure boundless longevity;
The principle of longevity
is exhausted in this.
If there are those who desire to recklessly indulge their desires,
who consider themselves enlightened and knowledgeable about fate,
who are not attached to heterodox doctrines,
who indulge their emotions and exert their strength to the utmost,
and do not seek long life,
upon hearing these words,
it would be like wind passing through their ears,
or lightning flashing before their eyes;
it would be insufficient to enlighten them.
Even if their bodies wither amidst lingering pleasures,
and their breath expires amidst fine silks,
and they are content with this,
how can one possibly tell them about the matter of nourishing life?
Not only will they not accept it,
but they will even call it demonic nonsense.
To expect them to believe it
is like giving a clear mirror to a blind person,
or entertaining a deaf man with silk and bamboo music."
Bàopǔzi 抱朴子 said:
"The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is life,
which is what brings forth good things.
Therefore, among the things that Daoists hold most secret and value most highly,
nothing surpasses the methods of longevity.
Hence, they are transmitted with a blood oath;
transmitting them to the wrong person
is a sin punishable by Heaven.
Xiān Shī (先師, my late teacher) did not dare to lightly impart these practices to others.
Only to those who sought them with utmost diligence,
would he teach them, and even then, he would select only the most refined individuals.
How much less, then, to those who neither desired nor sought,
or whose seeking was not earnest,
could he display and peddle these teachings?
For those whose destiny does not align with immortality,
even if they saw groups of immortals in the world every day,
they would still insist that those were a different species of human,
or that such things were unique occurrences in the world.
Some would even call them transformations of ghosts and demons,
or claim that they just happened to naturally.
How could they ever be willing to say it was the result of cultivation?
If one's heart does not believe,
even if Chì Sōng Zǐ (赤鬆子) and Wáng Qiáo (王喬) whispered in their ear,
they would still regard it as deceptive falsehood.
However, sometimes there are those who recognize and believe,
but suffer from not being able to diligently seek out a wise teacher.
Those who understand the most essential and obtain the true Dao,
are truly very rare,
and cannot be encountered hastily.
However, those who know it,
may just be few in number,
but have never been completely absent from the world.
It's because those who seek it are not broad and sincere enough.
Those with a destiny for immortality,
are bound to encounter them.
However, there are those who seek and do not find,
There is nothing that one obtains without seeking.
In the world, there are indeed deceitful and false people who scheme for money
and steal the title of "Daoist."
They are too numerous to count.
However, these sorts of people do not consider themselves to be completely ignorant.
They all roughly reveal some ability,
or falsely sell a reputation,
adding to it by concealing evil and embellishing falsehoods.
And those lovers of strange things,
who do not recognize their truth or falsity,
merely increase their inquiries,
taking delusion upon themselves.
And they restrict and control them,
preventing them from acting,
and widely search for strange scholars and unusual people,
and tell them,
"The Dao is exhausted here."
Misleading those who have aspiration is not a few;
it is lamentable and enraging.

Or, upon hearing of someone who understands how to dissipate the Five Clouds, fly the Eight Stones, turn the Nine Elixirs, smelt gold and silver, produce Water Jade, transform cinnabar into azurite, congeal frost and snow in a divine furnace, or gather *lingzhi* on Mount Sōngyuè,
then many denigrate them, saying,
"Only Chìsōng Wáng Qiáo knew this method.
If people of the present age claim to know it,
they are all false."
Then those with shallow views
do not perceive that these words are made with deceit and falsehood,
and thus cease their intention to seek afar.
Alas,
This is truly something to lament!
The sundial flies swiftly,
briefly young, then suddenly old,
so exceedingly rapid,
it can be likened to nothing.
A hundred years of life
is merely thirty thousand-plus days.
In infancy and weakness, one knows nothing;
in decline and old age, joy and pleasure are abandoned together.
From youthful ignorance to senile confusion,
subtracting several decades,
and with dangers, hardships, worries, and illnesses
following one another in succession,
the years spent in this world
roughly diminish by half.
Considering that one attains a hundred years,
with joy, laughter, and peace,
it is still no more than fifty or sixty years,
vanished in an instant.
With sorrow, worry, and senile confusion,
it amounts to six or seven thousand days.
A glance around and it is all over!
Moreover, concerning one who lives a full hundred years,
is there even one in ten thousand?
Thinking deeply about it,
one cannot laugh at the summer insect or morning mushroom.
This is indeed the utmost sadness for those who do not understand the Dao.
There is a saying in the village:
People in this world,
lose one day after another,
like leading an ox or sheep to the slaughterhouse.
With each step forward,
they get closer and closer to death.
This analogy may be crude,
but it is a true principle.
The reason why enlightened people do not worry about death
is not that they do not desire to live,
but that they know there is no art to escape death,
and empty worry is
of no use.
Therefore, it is said that they are happy with Heaven and know their fate,
and therefore do not worry;
it is not that they do not desire to live long.
Jī Gōng offered to substitute himself for King Wǔ,
and Zhòng Ní dragged his staff with sorrowful thoughts.
This shows that even sages do not rejoice in a quick death.
Common people, seeing Zhuāng Zhōu's parable of the great dream,
then compete to propagate theories that equalize life and death.
This is generally perverse artifice,
superficially making contradictory statements,
all of which are what Zhòng Ní condemned as destructive sophistry.
Now, examining those who have such talks,
when afflicted with illness, they rush to acupuncture,
and when facing danger, they are extremely afraid of death.
However, this is a common fault of the late generations:
not valuing true belief,
To govern with the books of philosophers while turning one's back on the classics and imperial edicts,
if one does not utter clever and ingenious arguments against reason,
then one is called simple and rustic;
this is not the learning of Lǎo Zhuāng.
Therefore, lacking substance, they attract common and vulgar followers,
and consequently drift along with untenable arguments,
unable to return to the right path.
Lǎozǐ took long life and prolonged vision as his pursuit,
while Zhuāng Zhōu valued wagging his tail in the mud,
not wanting to be a turtle caught in a net,
or an ox adorned with embroidery.
He was hungry and sought grain from Hé Hóu.
From this, we know that he could not equate life and death.
Later scholars cannot investigate the real and the false.
Leaning heavily on a single phrase,
isn't that absurd?
Moreover, going deep beneath the nine springs,
the long night is endless,
first becoming food for ants,
and finally merging with dust and earth.
This makes one feel deeply saddened and feverish,
unable to stop sighing.
If one's heart has a desire for life,
how can one not abandon unimportant matters,
in order to cultivate the mysterious and profound work?
If one does not believe it, then so be it.
But those who believe it
still suffer from not completely shedding worldly desires,
But they cannot focus solely on cultivating life,
but rather engage in it during the leisure time left over from managing worldly affairs.
Therefore, those who do engage in it
often begin too late and accomplish little.
What people eagerly pursue
are power, profit, and desires.
If my body is not whole,
even high office and great authority,
mountains of gold and jade,
and countless beauties
are not mine.
Therefore, superior scholars first engage in the matter of longevity.
Longevity certainly allows one to be unrestrained.
If one does not ascend to the heavens and depart,
one can still live as an earthly immortal among humans.
If, like Péng Zǔ and Lǎo Zǐ,
one lives only a few hundred years among people,
without losing the joys of human reason,
and then slowly ascends to the heavens,
it is also a great achievement.
However, a good teacher is absolutely necessary.
If one cannot adequately serve the teacher,
there is no way to succeed.
Formerly, the Hàn Empress Dowager, from Xiàhóu Shèng, received instruction in the *Shàngshū*.
She gifted Shèng one hundred *jīn* of gold,
and other gifts were too numerous to count.
And when Shèng died,
she further bestowed upon Shèng's family two million *qián*,
For Shèng, he wore plain clothes for one hundred days.
When Emperor Chéngdì was in the Eastern Palace,
he received the *Analects* from Zhāng Yǔ.
After ascending the throne,
he bestowed upon Yǔ the rank of Guānnèi Marquis,
with a fief of one thousand households,
appointed him Gūanglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Light),
and gifted him one hundred *jīn* of gold.
Later, he was promoted to Chancellor,
and advanced to the rank of Ānchāng Marquis.
In his old age, he requested to retire,
and was granted a comfortable carriage with a team of four horses,
one hundred *jīn* of gold,
and tens of thousands of coins.
When Yǔ fell ill,
the emperor personally visited and inquired after him,
personally bowing beneath Yǔ's bed.
When Emperor Zhāngdì was in the Eastern Palace,
he received the *Classic of Filial Piety* from Huán Róng.
After the emperor ascended the throne,
he appointed Róng as Tàicháng Shàngqīng (Grand Master of Ceremonies).
The emperor visited Róng's residence,
ordering Róng to sit facing east,
and providing a table and walking stick.
He gathered hundreds of officials and Róng's disciples and students,
and the emperor personally held his text and lectured.
He bestowed upon Róng the rank of Guānnèi Marquis,
with a fief of five thousand households.
Jí Róng bìng,
the emperor visited his home,
entering the lane and alighting from his carriage,
holding his scroll and hastening forward,
as a disciple would.
When Róng passed away,
the emperor wore plain clothes for Róng.
All these gentlemen,
were not able to attack cities and fight in the fields,
or repulse enemies and expand territories,
hang up banners and show their loyalty,
pacify the Qílián region,
contribute original achievements,
or display their prowess in remote regions.
They merely relied on their knowledge of one classic,
and propagated its chapters and verses,
and were seen as worthy of respect,
so grandly and greatly,
they were only able to speak the leftover words of the dead.
The nobility of the emperor
still humbled himself to respectfully serve them.
In the world, there are perhaps those who wish to try to cultivate the way to immortality,
but are unwilling to be humble to a teacher,
and are impolite and hurried,
seeking the essential secrets.
How can they possibly obtain them?
Moreover, what benefit does a scholar's respectful demeanor and willingness to run errands
have to the teacher's own welfare?
But if it is not like this,
then their heart is not sincere;
if their heart is not sincere,
then the person informing them will not exert themselves fully;
if the person informing them does not exert themselves fully,
then how can the secret doctrines be fully obtained?
If one cannot but show them something superficial,
how can that be sufficient to achieve the merit of immortality?
There are also people whose skin is fond of pleasure
and whose sincerity in believing in the Dao
is not rooted in their heart and spirit.
Having desires and wants,
they outwardly pretend to be respectful.
After several days,
laziness emerges.
If they encounter a wise teacher,
who wishes to carefully observe the changes in the newcomer's attitude,
they will test them with prolonged delay,
and therefore not tell them
in order to gauge their will.
In that case, such a person's
true feelings and hypocrisy will be revealed,
and in the end, they cannot be taught;
even if taught, they cannot be told the complete truth;
if the complete truth is not spoken, then it is of no benefit to them.
Chén Ānshì,
at the age of thirteen,
was a guest of Guàn Shūběn.
First obtain the Dao of Immortality.
Shū Běnnián, at the age of seventy with a white head,
morning and night would bow to Ān Shì, saying,
"The Dao is esteemed, and virtue is valued.
He who obtains the Dao first becomes the teacher.
I dare not tire of upholding the etiquette of a disciple."
Thereupon, Ān Shì told him the essential method,
and then he resumed his immortal journey.
Now, in life, one first receives spirit from Heaven and Earth,
and then receives vitality and blood from parents.
However, without obtaining a wise teacher,
to instruct one in the Dao of passing through the world,
there is no way to avoid death.
Chiseling stone leaves residual heat,
yet one's years and life force have already withered.
From this it can be argued that,
the grace of a wise teacher,
truly exceeds that of Heaven and Earth,
and is more important than that of parents.
How can we not revere it?
How can we not seek it?"
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"The ancients were of genuine and upright quality,
valuing action and disdaining words.
Therefore, those who governed did not value literary debate,
and those who cultivated the Dao did not esteem eloquent speech.
As customs decline and become degenerate,

For beginners,

Moreover, it is also human nature to find satisfaction in rich content from beginning to end.
Therefore, later adepts,

Their ultimate true secrets,

Common and lowly disciples,

jiē gè suí qí yòngxīn zhī shūmì,
the length of their endured hardship,

Throughout thousands of years,

The ingredients of the medicine,

Therefore, the Daoists in the world,

But achieving longevity lies in the great medicine,

In the past, during the Qín and Hàn dynasties,

How much more so ordinary people,

whose bodies are not nourished,

Or perhaps there are some busybodies,

They concoct strange medicines in collaboration,

Coming to old age with no benefit,

Or, an entire household knocks their heads

In the end, they do not repent,

If they used this diligence

How is this different from going to old age tilling a stony field

Though their effort is exhausted,

This is what is meant by heading to Chǔ (楚) but taking the road to Yān (燕);
though the horse is good, it will not arrive,

Perhaps there are those who are by nature trusting and delight in trusting others,

their range of knowledge is inherently narrow,

Later generations are foolish and shallow.
Becoming interested in one person,

However, mediocre people and petty fellows

Their reputation exceeds their reality,

They harbor inner greed and corruption,

When something is requested of them,

As if the secret knowledge they possess is profound and unobtainable.
If something is requested of them,

Intentionally making those who are unaware

Thereupon, their hearts of sincere belief

But they idly wasted years,

Those teachers initially deceived them with sincerity,

Ignorant within themselves,

They often wander among the common customs,

This often happens because of such people,

Every time I see these fellows

Although the net of Heaven is wide-meshed,

It is only those who are mistakenly led astray that are pitiable.
The people of the world mostly pursue empty reputations

Seeking timber reaching the sky;

Alas!
Future scholars,
Although they should make seeking a teacher their priority,

Men of narrow minds,
With shallow conduct and meager virtue,

Are not sufficient for the path of becoming an accomplished person.

Think deeply about its purpose,
"Do not let them labor in vain."

is an image of a nation.
The position of the chest and abdomen
is like a palace.
The arrangement of the four limbs
is like the suburbs and borders.
The divisions of the bones and joints
are like the various officials.
The spirit (shén) is like the ruler,
the blood is like the ministers,
the qi (qì) is like the people.
Therefore, knowing how to govern the body
is knowing how to govern the state.
Loving the people is how to secure the state,
nourishing the qi (qì) is how to preserve the body.
If the people are scattered, the state will perish;
if the qi (qì) is exhausted, the body will die.
The dead cannot be brought back to life,
the lost cannot be preserved.
Therefore, the perfect person eliminates troubles before they arise,
treats illnesses before they manifest,
and practices medicine before anything happens,
not chasing after what has already passed.
The people are difficult to nourish and easily endangered;
there is nothing that is not done.
Gathering and digging medicinal herbs,
toiling laboriously in the mountains and marshes,
decocting and preparing them,
all require physical strength,
climbing dangers and traversing perils.
diligently working day and night,
without an unwavering determination,
it cannot be sustained for long.
As for wanting to achieve the golden elixir and ascend to heaven,
the ingredients for that great medicine,
all require monetary value,
impossible to procure all at once.
One must again rely on farming, herding, and trading to seek capital,
accumulating diligence over the years,
only then can they be combined.
And on the day of combining the ingredients,
one must again be ritually pure and clean,
severing contact with human affairs.
With all these difficulties,
one must also add to it the contemplation of spirits and guarding of Oneness,
repelling evil and protecting the body,
constantly like a ruler governing the state,
or a military general awaiting the enemy,
only then can one attain the merit of longevity.
With intelligence and great wisdom,
capable of managing the world and benefiting society,
and cultivating this matter,
And when there were guests at their seats,
there was one host talking to the guest,
and another host welcoming the guest at the door,
and another host fishing by the water's edge.
The guest could not distinguish which was the real host.
The master said, 'Guarding the One should be combined with cultivating the Bright Mirror.'"
When the mirror way is accomplished, it can divide the form into dozens of people,
with clothing and appearance
all alike."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The master said, 'If you desire longevity,
you should diligently take the great medicine.
If you want to gain spiritual powers,
you should use gold-water to divide your form.
When the form is divided, you will naturally see the three souls and seven spirits within your body,
and the heavenly spirits and earthly deities
can all be met and seen.
The gods of mountains and rivers
can all be commanded and employed.'"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Life is to be cherished,
death is to be feared.
However, those who seek longevity, nurture their nature, and avoid death,
none have not begun with diligence
and ultimately achieved it through long-term practice.
After the Way is accomplished,
there is practically nothing to do.
Before it is accomplished,
"The Way of the Mysterious One
is also an essential method.
There is nothing it does not ward off.
It has the same efficacy as being one with the Realized.
The reason why I named the first chapter of my Inner Chapters *Chàng Xuán* (暢玄, Flourishing Mystery)
is precisely because of this.
Guarding Xuán Yī is even easier than guarding the True One.
The True One has a name, length, clothing color, and eye description,
but Xuán Yī is merely seeing this.
Initially seek it in the middle of the day,
which is called 'knowing the white and guarding the black,'
those who desire death but cannot die.
However, one must first abstain and purify oneself for a hundred days
before one can hope to seek and obtain it.
It takes no more than three or four days to obtain it.
Once obtained and guarded,
it will never leave again.
Guarding Xuán Yī,
contemplate one's body,
dividing it into three people.
Once three people are seen,
add to them again,
up to several tens of people,
all like oneself,
hiding them and revealing them,
all with their own secret formulas.
This is what is called the Way of Dividing the Body.
This is how Zuǒ Jūn, Jì Zǐxùn, and Gé Xiān Gōng were able to be in dozens of places in one day.
all evils will flee far away.
If one suddenly and accidentally forgets to guard the One,
one will be harmed by a hundred ghosts.
Or if one is lying down and experiencing a nightmare,
one should immediately go out to the middle courtyard, look at the Assistant Star (fǔ xīng),
clench one's fists, guard the One,
The ghost will then depart.
If there is overcast or rainy weather,
simply remain in the room
and face north, mentally visualizing the Fǔxīng.
If one is besieged by bandits or enemies
and there is no way out,
quickly enter the yin position of the Liùjiǎ (六甲, Six Jia),
prostrate oneself and guard the One.
Then, the five weapons will be unable to harm one.
One who can guard the One,
traveling ten thousand miles,
entering military encampments,
crossing great rivers,
need not divine the days or choose the hours.
Starting construction or moving dwelling,
entering a new house,
one need no longer consult Kānyú (堪輿, geomancy) or the astral almanac,
and need not avoid Tài Suì (太歲, Grand Duke Jupiter), Tài Yīn jiāngjūn (太陰將軍, General Great Yin), the Yuè Jiàn (月建, Month Construction), Shā hào (煞耗, Killing and Consumption) deities,
or the annual life's taboos.
In the end, one will not encounter misfortune or blame.
This is a method that previous sages have tested and found effective."
Bàopǔzǐ (抱朴子) said:
And each is effective.
However, some involve visualizing thousands of things for self-defense,
Which are mostly troublesome and difficult,
Enough to greatly weary one's mind.
If one knows the Dao of guarding the One,
Then all such things can be discarded.
Therefore, it is said that being able to know the One, then all things are completed.
Receiving the true oral instruction of the One,
all have clear texts.
One must smear the blood of a white sacrificial animal,
and receive it on a day when the "kingly phase" (wáng xiāng) is in effect.
One must use white silk and white silver as a pledge,
engrave a golden contract and divide it.
Lightly speaking of it and falsely transmitting it
will render its spirit ineffective.
If a person can guard the One,
the One will also guard the person.
Therefore, a white blade will find no place to apply its sharpness,
and a hundred harms will find no place to harbor their evil.
Dwelling in defeat, one can achieve success;
in danger, one can be uniquely safe.
If one is in the midst of a ghost temple,
beneath mountains and forests,
in a place of great epidemic,
in the space between tombs,
in a den of tigers and wolves,
in a place of snakes and vipers,
if one guards the One without slackening,
then one can communicate with the spirits;
reducing desires and moderating diet,
then the One will remain and preserve breath;
when a naked blade is at your neck,
thinking of the One, you will gain life;
knowing the One is not difficult,"
The difficulty lies in maintaining it to the end;
Maintaining it without losing it,
One can be boundless;
On land, it wards off fierce beasts;
In water, it repels dragons;
One will not fear wǎngliǎng (spirits of mountains and streams),
Or insects bearing poison;
Ghosts dare not approach,
Blades dare not strike.
This is the general outline of the Great One."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I heard it from my teacher,
That in the various Daoist scriptures,
Methods of contemplation, visualization, and meditation,
That can repel evil and defend oneself,
There are thousands of methods.
Such as concealing the shadow and hiding the form,
And guarding the form to attain non-birth,
Nine transformations, twelve transmutations, twenty-four lives, and so on,
Visualizing and seeing the various deities within the body,
And methods of internal observation to make them visible,
Are too numerous to count,
engraved on golden tablets,
sealed with purple clay,
and stamped with the Central Seal."
I heard from my late teacher:
"The One is in the midst of the Great Abyss of the North Pole,
in front is a Bright Hall,
behind it is the Crimson Palace;
lofty and majestic is the flowery canopy,
golden towers are domed;
on the left is the Dipper Handle, on the right is the Chief Star,
turbulent waves rise into the air;
dark fungus covers the cliffs,
crimson grasses are hazy;
white jade is jagged and towering,
the sun and moon cast their light;
passing through fire and crossing water,
traversing the dark and wading through the yellow;
city walls are intertwined,
curtains and canopies are adorned with jade;
dragons and tigers stand in rows as guards,
spirits and men are beside it;
neither giving nor taking,
the One is at peace in its place;
neither slow nor fast,

if one can be at leisure and ease,

guarding the One and preserving Truth,
passing Kōngtóng,
receiving the Scripture of Nature from Master Guǎngchéngzǐ.
He traveled north to Hóngdī,

Returning, he ascended Mount Wángwū,

He arrived at Mount Éméi,

Huángrén said:
"Since you already rule the four seas,
yet still desire to seek longevity,
is that not greedy?
Their mutual interactions cannot be fully explained,

As for the methods of immortality,
there is only the golden elixir;
As for preserving the body and warding off evil,
there is only the True Oneness,
therefore the ancients particularly valued them.
The Immortal Scripture says:
The Nine-Turn Elixir,
The Golden Liquid Scripture,
The Secret of Guarding the One,
are all within the five cities of Kunlun,
stored in jade boxes,
for a woman, it is six *fēn* long.
It is either in the lower *dāntián* two *cùn* and four *fēn* below the navel,
or in the middle *dāntián* in the Crimson Palace and Golden Tower below the heart,
or between a person's eyebrows.
Moving back one *cùn* is the Míngtáng Hall,
two *cùn* is the Dòngfáng Chamber,
three cun is the upper *dāntián*.
This is what the Daoists value,
in every generation swearing an oath and orally transmitting its name.
One can create yin and generate yang,
calculating the progression of cold and heat.
Spring obtains one to sprout,
summer obtains one to grow,
autumn obtains one to harvest,
winter obtains one to store.
Its greatness cannot be measured by the six directions,
its smallness cannot be compared to a hair.
Once, the Yellow Emperor, Huángdì, traveled east to Qīngqiū,
passing Mount Fēng,
where he met Master Zǐfǔ
and received the Inner Writings of the Three Sovereigns,
to summon and command the myriad spirits.
He traveled south to Yuánlǒng, where a shade-giving Jiàn Wood was planted,
observing the place where the hundred spirits ascended,
gathering the flowers of Ruògān,
and drinking the water of the red cliffs.
He traveled west and met Master Zhōnghuángzǐ,
receiving the methods of Nine Additions,
Earth attains One and becomes peaceful,
Man attains One and lives,
Spirit attains One and becomes efficacious.
Gold sinks, feathers float,
mountains stand, rivers flow,
look but cannot be seen,
Listen to it, and you cannot hear it.
Preserve it, and it exists;
Neglect it, and it vanishes.
Turn towards it, and there is good fortune;
Turn away from it, and there is misfortune.
Protect it, and there will be boundless blessings and longevity;
Lose it, and life dwindles and vitality exhausts.
Lǎojūn said:
"Dim and indistinct,

Indistinct and dim,

Therefore, the Immortal Scripture says:
"If you wish for longevity,
guarding the One should be clear.
Think of the One to the point of hunger,
the One will give you food;

the One will give you drink."
The One has a name and appearance.
For a man, it is nine *fēn* long;
and the tiger will not dare to rise.

burn cattle and sheep horns,

Heaven attains One and becomes clear,

inhale three hundred and sixty breaths,

Stamp them with the seal in the opposite direction,

Carrying this seal while traveling in the mountains and forests

seal them with the seal,

Someone asked:

This rhinoceros lives in deep mountains,

If a person is hit by a poisoned arrow and is about to die,

The reason why the *tōngtiān* rhinoceros is able to kill poisons is that

If a person finds it,
jiān tóng zhe niú mǎ wū zuǒ yòu qián hòu jí zhū lán shàng, (can also be placed on the left, right, front, and back of cattle and horse pens, as well as pigsties,)

Huò wèn yuē: (Someone asked:)

they will be startled and retreat.
Therefore, the people of the South sometimes call the sky-penetrating rhinoceros horn the 'chicken-startling rhinoceros horn'.
The meaning is: 'You are not of the Gé lineage.'"

and on a *yīn* day, carry the female one.

is all said to be for those who are just beginning to learn the Dao.
Yáo Xiānshēng only took Sān Yáng Yè,

clear strings strum clamorously in unison,
Zheng dances swirl in confusion,
mournful flutes sound, reaching the clouds,
feathered canopies float on the ripples,
plucking fragrant blossoms from the orchid-filled gardens,
playing with red flowers in the pearl-paved pond,
climbing high, they gaze into the distance to forget a hundred worries,
overlooking the deep, they look down and embrace, forgetting the morning hunger,
entering banquets of brilliantly lit thousand gates,
leaving, they drive in carriages with bright red wheels of splendid adornment.
But when joy reaches its peak, sorrow gathers,
clouds move by it,
and rain is brought forth by it.
It contains the primordial unity,
and molds the two primary forces.
It breathes in and out the Great Beginning,
and forges and transforms countless kinds.
circling and returning through the twenty-eight constellations,
crafting and completing the chaotic darkness,
reins and guides the spiritual mechanism,
blows and breathes the four seasons,
silently encompasses profound stillness,
broadly displays brilliant splendor,
suppresses the turbid and raises the clear,
governs the Hé Hé and the Wèi River,
increasing it, it does not overflow,
diminishing it, it is not exhausted,
giving to it, it does not flourish,
taking from it, it does not wither.
Therefore, where the profound (xuán) resides,
its joy is inexhaustible.
Where the profound (xuán) departs,
the vessel is ruined, and the spirit vanishes.
Now, the five tones and eight sounds,
clear shāng and flowing zhǐ,
are what diminish hearing.
Fresh, flowery and vibrant colors,
luxuriant and brilliantly radiant,
are what injure sight.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Xuán,
is the primal ancestor of nature
and the great progenitor of all differences.
So subtle and obscure is its depth,
therefore it is called 'microscopic'.
So continuous and far-reaching is its distance,
therefore it is called 'marvelous'.
In its height, it crowns the nine heavens;
in its vastness, it encompasses the eight corners of the universe.
It shines brighter than the sun and moon,
and is swifter than a lightning flash.
Sometimes it glitters and vanishes in an instant,
sometimes it surges and flows like a shooting star,
sometimes it shimmers in the deep stillness,
sometimes it drifts like a misty cloud.
It becomes existence by relying on myriad forms,
and becomes non-existence by relying on deep silence.
It descends into the great darkness below,
and ascends to the utmost limits of the stars above.
Gold and stone cannot compare to its hardness,
nor can morning dew equal its softness.
It is square but not measured by a square,
round but not drawn by a compass.
Its coming cannot be seen,
its going cannot be traced.
Heaven is made high by it,
Earth is made low by it,
